clinicalPearls: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is a state of target-organ resistance to aldosterone, so despite very high aldosterone the kidney cannot retain sodium normally
The autosomal dominant (renal) form is due to loss-of-function variants in NR3C2, the mineralocorticoid receptor, and tends to be milder and to improve with age
The autosomal recessive (systemic) form is due to loss-of-function variants in the epithelial sodium channel subunits (SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G) and is more severe and persistent
The biochemical signature is salt wasting with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, alongside markedly elevated renin and aldosterone
In the systemic form, sodium loss also affects sweat, salivary glands and colon, and recurrent respiratory symptoms can mimic cystic fibrosis
It is effectively the mirror image of Liddle syndrome, with an underactive rather than overactive sodium channel pathway
Management rests on generous sodium supplementation and control of hyperkalaemia; the recessive systemic form typically needs lifelong high-dose salt replacement
reference.pathophysiology: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is caused by failure of aldosterone signalling in the distal nephron. In the dominant renal form, loss-of-function variants in the mineralocorticoid receptor gene NR3C2 blunt the response to aldosterone; in the recessive systemic form, loss-of-function variants in the epithelial sodium channel subunits prevent sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct and in other epithelia. Because sodium cannot be reabsorbed and the electrochemical gradient for potassium and hydrogen secretion is lost, the kidney wastes salt while retaining potassium and hydrogen ion, producing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis. The salt loss and hypovolaemia strongly stimulate renin and aldosterone, but the target tissues cannot respond, so the very high hormone levels coexist with continued salt wasting.
additionalDifferentials: Primary adrenal insufficiency (aldosterone deficiency, e.g. salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia)
Transient pseudohypoaldosteronism secondary to urinary tract infection or obstructive uropathy in infants
Cystic fibrosis (salt loss with respiratory disease, mimicking the systemic form)
additionalInvestigations: Serum sodium, potassium and bicarbonate to document salt-wasting hyperkalaemic acidosis
Plasma renin and aldosterone (both markedly elevated)
Urinary electrolytes to confirm renal sodium loss
Sweat chloride testing to assess systemic involvement and exclude cystic fibrosis
Renal tract imaging to exclude secondary/transient causes such as obstruction or infection
Molecular genetic testing of NR3C2 and the ENaC subunit genes
redFlags: Life-threatening neonatal salt-wasting crisis with severe hyperkalaemia
Recurrent respiratory infections in the systemic form
reference.prognosis: The dominant renal form often attenuates with age and may need little treatment in adulthood, whereas the recessive systemic form is severe, persists lifelong, and requires continuous salt supplementation and careful management of hyperkalaemia.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as adrenal insufficiency and giving mineralocorticoid replacement, which is ineffective because the defect is resistance, not deficiency
Failing to distinguish the transient secondary form (infection/obstruction) from inherited disease
Overlooking systemic salt loss and confusing the recessive form with cystic fibrosis
Underestimating the very large sodium requirements of the systemic form
Not appreciating the mode of inheritance when counselling families
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
management: Correct salt wasting with generous sodium chloride supplementation, the mainstay of treatment particularly in the recessive systemic form
Manage hyperkalaemia with dietary potassium restriction and cation-exchange resins, and treat acute hyperkalaemia promptly
Correct the metabolic acidosis with alkali where required
Recognise that mineralocorticoids are ineffective because the defect is receptor or channel resistance, not hormone deficiency
In the systemic form, manage cutaneous, respiratory and other epithelial salt loss and distinguish the picture from cystic fibrosis
Regular monitoring of electrolytes, hydration and growth, with paediatric nephrology input
Genetic counselling and family testing (NR3C2 in the dominant renal form; ENaC subunit genes in the recessive systemic form)
